title: Where is wisdom? (Job 28)
hook: men mine for silver and gold, but wisdom isn't found in the earth
carry: the fear of the lord is wisdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job carving a hope in rock. Your word was redeemer, and your line, my redeemer lives. Who did you stand up for? Day four hundred forty-seven.

Chapter twenty-eight of Job begins underground. The arguing between Job and his friends suddenly stops, and a poem starts, about miners. They push back the darkness, it says. They cut shafts in places no traveler goes. They hang on ropes, swinging, far from other people. They turn mountains over by the roots and find sapphires in the stone and gold in the dust. No bird knows these paths; no vulture's eye has seen them. No lion has walked them. Humans, the poem says, can dig their way to almost anything. Almost.
screen: `SHAFTS CUT INTO ROCK.` → `MINERS ON ROPES.` → `HUMANS CAN REACH ALMOST ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it." Silver has a place. Gold has a place. Then the question that names today: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?" You can dig for it, but "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me." You can't buy it either. The poem piles up the treasures of the ancient world, gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, pearls, topaz, and sets them all aside: "the price of wisdom is above rubies." Even death and destruction say they've only heard rumors of it. So where is it? "God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof." Then the last verse, in which God speaks to humankind: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding." The Hebrew word is yirah. It can mean fear, and it can mean awe and reverence, the feeling of standing in front of something far greater than you; readers often hear the second here. Notice what the poem is doing in the middle of Job's story. Job and his friends have spent chapter after chapter trying to work out exactly why he's suffering, each sure he has the answer. This poem quietly says: nobody can dig that out. Real wisdom isn't a fact you extract. It starts with awe, and with turning away from harm. Scholars debate who speaks the poem, Job or the book's narrator; it reads like a pause, a breath in the argument. And it sounds a theme you'll hear again when Proverbs opens.
screen: `A VEIN FOR THE SILVER` · `THE DEPTH SAITH, IT IS NOT IN ME` · `ABOVE RUBIES` · `GOD KNOWETH THE PLACE` · then, large: `THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THAT IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for wisdom in one conversation. Before the sit, choose a conversation you'll have today, at work, at home, on the phone. During the sit, picture it. Who's there? Where do you usually rush, or argue, or try to win? Now picture going in with a little awe instead: listening for what you don't already know. Let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom, in your own words or with the poem's last line. If you don't, set the simple intention to listen like a miner looks for a vein. The bell holds the time.
Where is wisdom? Job chapter twenty-eight's question: humans can mine almost anything, but wisdom begins in awe of God.
Your line: the fear of the Lord is wisdom. Today, in one conversation, listen for the thing you don't know yet, before you say the thing you do. Day four hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray for wisdom before decisions and study, and some read Job 28 as a meditation on the limits of what human cleverness can dig out.

yirah can mean fear, and it can also mean awe and reverence.

fork.setup: you want wisdom badly, and you have a fortune in gold, sapphires and pearls. what does the poem say happens if you try to buy it?
options: it goes to the highest bidder.
no treasure can pay for it.
fork.reveal: "the price of wisdom is above rubies." gold, onyx, sapphire, coral and pearls can't buy it. only God knows where it is.

original.note: Hebrew: the fear of the Lord, meaning awe and reverence. Job 28:28 uses Adonai, Lord, here.

trapdoor: what you thought: wisdom means being smart or well-read.
what it means: humans can mine almost anything, but wisdom starts with awe of God and turning from harm.
what a scholar hears: an interlude poem whose speaker is debated, ending in yirat Adonai, a theme Proverbs returns to.
